query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In conventional corrosion-resistant steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, an intentional pre-oxidation treatment that promotes chromium segregation to the surface will form a denser and more stable Cr2O3-rich passivation layer, thereby mechanistically enhancing the corrosion resistance compared to untreated steels.
generation.material_initial_state: Conventional steel alloys with a standard microstructure and naturally forming, but less controlled, passivating surface layers containing elements like Cr, Ni, and Mo.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary alloying element concentrations (especially Cr) and apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to induce selective Cr segregation at the surface.
generation.conditions: Simulated service environments typical of chemical-processing (e.g., acidic or alkaline solutions at elevated temperatures) and nuclear-power applications (moderate radiation and high-temperature conditions), with experiments conducted using potentiodynamic polarization and EIS.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stabilization of a dense, Cr2O3-rich passive film at the steel surface.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced corrosion resistance arises because chromium enriches the surface via selective oxidation during the pre-oxidation treatment, leading to a protective Cr2O3 layer that inhibits aggressive ion attack and limits further metal dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples that undergo the controlled pre-oxidation treatment, leading to increased Cr segregation, will exhibit higher polarization resistance, lower corrosion current densities, and more compact passive films (as indicated by XPS and EIS measurements) compared to untreated baseline samples.
generation.baseline: Untreated steel samples with standard alloy compositions and passivation layers formed under ambient oxidation conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under moderately aggressive chemical-processing solutions and nuclear-power simulation environments, and may not apply under extreme conditions (e.g., very high radiation flux or extreme temperatures) where additional degradation mechanisms dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of Cr in stabilizing passive films is supported by previous studies, uncertainties remain regarding the interaction with other alloying elements like Ni and Mo, and the influence of local microstructural variations on the effectiveness of Cr segregation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare sets of steel samples with a range of Cr concentrations. Subject one set to a controlled pre-oxidation treatment designed to promote Cr segregation and leave another set untreated as baseline. Expose both sets to simulated chemical-processing and nuclear power environment conditions. Perform in situ XPS to quantify the Cr2O3 content and morphology, potentiodynamic polarization tests to determine corrosion kinetics, and EIS to assess the passive film resistance.
measurements: XPS analysis of the surface oxide composition and thickness
Polarization resistance and corrosion current density from potentiodynamic tests
EIS measurements for passive film compactness and resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized, Cr-enriched samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in oxide film stability (i.e., no marked increase in Cr2O3 content and film compactness) and corrosion resistance (as measured by higher polarization resistance and lower corrosion rates) relative to the untreated baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Electrochemical experiments have demonstrated that the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating exhibits excellent corrosion resistance, and that the passivation film of the coating may play an important role. To prove this guess, chemical compositions of the passive film formed on the surface of the (CoCrFeNi)95Nb5 HEA coating after air oxidation were investigated by XPS. Figure 8 shows the XPS spectra of the passivation film on the surface of HEA coating in air. The full survey spectrum (Figure 8a) exhibits that the passivation film contains seven elements of Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Nb, O, and C []. The peaks of Ni 2p correspond to Ni and NiO (Figure 8b). The Co 2p peaks are determined as Co and CoO (Figure 8c). The peaks of Fe 2p are identified as Fe and Fe2O3 (Figure 7d). The Cr 2p peaks correspond to Cr2O3 (Figure 8e). Lastly, Nb2O5 (Figure 8f) is observed in the peaks of Nb 3d.

Corrosion in molten salts is affected by several factors such as thermodynamics of corrosion reactions, elemental activities in the salt and the alloy, impurities, and temperature gradients. For instance, moisture in the salt can lead to the formation of hydrofluoric acid which can interact with metallic structural alloys and cause elemental dissolution into the salt. Also, metallic impurities incorporated in the salt may undergo exchange reactions to leach the least noble element out of the alloy. Most engineering alloys used in nuclear applications contain reasonable amounts of Cr to provide protection against air oxidation, and typically, chromium is the most vulnerable alloying element to fluoride salt corrosion.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 9a describes the Nyquist plots of the H1, H2, H3 and H4 coatings in the 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution. The diameter of the capacitive semicircle of the H4 coating was larger than those of the other three coatings, also indicating a higher corrosion resistance of the H4 as compared to those of the H1, H2 and H3 coatings. The features of H2 coating are analogous to those of H1 coating where a depressed capacitive semicircle covers most of the high-frequency regions, with a straight line appearing at the low-frequency area. The occurrence of straight line in the Nyquist plots reveals that the diffusion of oxidation products plays a negative role in the kinetics of the dissolution of surface passive film [,,]. However, no apparent straight line in the Nyquist plots of the H3 and H4 coatings can be seen in the low-frequency region. The Nyquist plots for the H3 and H4 coatings under passivation conditions are characterized by a somewhat unfinished semi-circle, a feature which is potential-dependent. The diameter of the semicircle in the Nyquist plot becomes bigger with increasing the potential, suggesting a continuous growth in the corrosion resistance.

These results indicate that the resistance to pitting of the HEAs is determined exclusively by Cr, and the effect of other elements such as Ni and Co on the passivity is limited. If one compares the pitting potential with those of 304 SS [,], the pitting potential of 304 SS is higher than that in the present results despite having the same PRE, and it increased with the formation of the UFG structure. However, little difference in Epit was observed between the HPT and CG samples, which suggests that UFG formation by HPT has little impact on the protective properties of the passivation film and the corrosion resistance. Figure 11 shows the corresponding STEM images and elemental maps. The layer with a high O signal is considered to be the passivation film. A Cr-rich oxide layer was observed on both CG and HPT specimens, which indicates that a stable passivation film can form on both specimens and that Cr is the main passivation former. chosen.lever: systematic variation of key alloying elements that govern passive layer chemistry
chosen.technique: potentiodynamic polarization paired with in situ XPS to monitor oxide composition and evolution
chosen.conditions: controlled exposure to corrosive media replicating chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions (e.g., elevated temperature, acidic and chloride-rich aqueous environments)
chosen.why: This approach directly inverts the open mechanistic question by testing whether variations in alloying composition lead to predictable changes in passive oxide layer formation and consequently in corrosion resistance. It employs standard, well-established electrochemical and surface analytical methods under realistic service conditions to reveal the governing cause and to establish the boundaries of the hypothesis.

frame.system: Steels formulated for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, starting from a conventional alloy microstructure that features passivating surface layers formed by elements such as chromium, nickel, and molybdenum.
frame.goal: To establish a testable mechanistic explanation for the resistance to corrosion by identifying the role of alloying element segregation (or similar phenomena) in forming or stabilizing protective surface films under aggressive environments.
frame.limitation: The current lack of direct, controlled mechanistic studies linking microstructural changes (such as the formation of a specific passivation layer or localized ion enrichment) to observed corrosion resistance in these steels.
constraints: Must be a controlled study capable of directly testing the mechanism versus a baseline (e.g., untreated or standard steel samples)
The study should specify predicted observations relative to a baseline
The hypothesis should indicate clear boundaries (operational conditions under which it holds)
Supporting evidence from prior findings (e.g., passive layer behavior from previous corrosion studies) must be acknowledged
A defined falsification criterion must be provided
frame.regime: Simulated service environments typical of chemical-processing (e.g., acidic/alkaline solutions at elevated temperatures) and nuclear-power applications (e.g., high temperature, radiation exposure, and aggressive coolant chemistries)
prior_attempts: Empirical correlations between alloy composition and corrosion rate without direct causative evidence
Kinetic corrosion tests that did not resolve the micro-mechanistic role of surface film formation and stability

decision.trend: Early corrosion studies on multicomponent and high‐entropy alloys began by correlating alloy composition with performance, then moved to more sophisticated electrochemical and surface characterization methods (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization and scanning Kelvin probe) to unveil micro-galvanic effects and passive film formation. However, these efforts largely focused on non-steel systems or empirical kinetics without directly testing how localized enrichment of key alloying elements (like Cr, Ni, and Mo) contributes mechanistically to passivity.
decision.unsolved: There remains no direct, controlled mechanistic study linking the segregation of alloying elements and the consequent formation or stability of a passivating oxide layer in conventional steels used in aggressive chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments.
decision.lever: systematic variation of alloying element concentrations combined with controlled pre-oxidation treatments, employing potentiodynamic polarization and in situ XPS to monitor passive oxide formation
decision.why: This approach directly follows the trend from empirical corrosion testing to targeted surface studies seen in earlier work. By deliberately adjusting the key alloying additions that are hypothesized to enrich the protective layer, the experiment can isolate the effect of element segregation. It also aligns with the open-question niche by providing a controlled study that distinguishes the mechanistic role of passivation—in simulated chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions—relative to baseline treatments. A failure to observe a significant, composition-dependent stabilization of the oxide film would falsify the hypothesis.
